}
plot_packages <- c("ggplot2", "igraph", "ggraph", "tidygraph")
## the functions need coglasso from version 1.1.0

# Introduction

The network functions of `r Biocpkg("exposomeSC")` estimate, for one cell type,
a sparse graph over transcripts of that cell type and the features of a second
omic layer that is measured once per donor, such as metabolites in plasma. An
edge joins two features that remain associated across the donors given the
other features of the graph: a non-zero entry of a penalised estimate of the
precision matrix.

The functions are exploratory. An edge is a regularised conditional association
under a Gaussian graphical model of transformed data. It is not a biochemical
interaction and not a causal relation, and which edges are found depends on the
transform, the penalties and the number of donors.

These functions answer a different question from `run_sc_exwas()`, which tests
one exposure against one gene at a time, and they do not use its results. They
share the container and the pseudobulk step with it.

The vignette runs on the INCOV data of the package: blood cells of 43 patients
with COVID-19 [@su2020] and metabolites measured in their plasma at the same
blood draw (`?incov_pbmc_subset`). With 43 donors and at most 14 cells per
donor and cell type, the networks below show how the functions are called and
what they return. They are not findings.

The estimators come from `r CRANpkg("glasso")` and `r CRANpkg("coglasso")`, and
the plots need `r CRANpkg("ggplot2")`, `r CRANpkg("igraph")`,
`r CRANpkg("ggraph")` and `r CRANpkg("tidygraph")`. exposomeSC only suggests
these packages; a chunk that needs one of them is run when it is installed.

# Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("exposomeSC")
```

# The data

```{r data, message=FALSE}
library(exposomeSC)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
x <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "incov_pbmc_subset.rds",
    package = "exposomeSC"))
table(x$cell_type)
plasma <- metadata(x)$plasma_metabolites
dim(plasma)
table(metadata(x)$metabolite_info$super_pathway)
```

The second layer is a matrix with one row per donor. Its rows are matched to
the donors of the cells by name, never by position:

```{r donors}
identical(rownames(plasma), rownames(exposureData(x)))
```

The examples use a small panel: 12 interferon-stimulated genes, because the
donors had a viral infection, and ten metabolites of amino-acid pathways, on
the log2 scale.

```{r features}
interferon <- c("IFI6", "ISG15", "MX1", "IFITM3", "STAT1", "XAF1", "EPSTI1",
    "LY6E", "IRF7", "ISG20", "MX2", "EIF2AK2")
panel <- c("kynurenine", "kynurenate", "arginine", "methionine", "sarcosine",
    "spermidine", "5-oxoproline", "3-indoxyl sulfate", "indolepropionate",
    "dimethylarginine (SDMA + ADMA)")
metabolites <- log2(plasma[, panel])
colnames(metabolites)[10] <- "dimethylarginine"
```

The calls of this vignette differ in the cell type and the estimator only, so
they go through one helper:

```{r helper}
network <- function(celltype, ...) {
    run_celltype_network(x, metabolites = metabolites, celltype = celltype,
        covariates = c("age", "sex_male"), genes = interferon,
        transform = "log_cpm", ...)
}
```

# The transform of the counts

The functions sum the raw counts of the cell type within each donor and
transform the sums. The default, `transform = "vst"`, is the
variance-stabilising transformation of `r Biocpkg("DESeq2")`, which needs
1,000 genes with a mean normalised count above 5. Fourteen cells per donor do
not give that many; the number of genes with a mean raw count above 5 is:

```{r depth}
monocytes <- assay(donor_pseudobulk(x)[["Monocyte"]], "counts")
sum(rowMeans(monocytes) > 5)
```

A call with the default therefore stops. It does not switch to another
transform, because the same call would then give different networks on
different data or machines:

```{r vst, error=TRUE, eval=has("glasso", "DESeq2")}
run_celltype_network(x, metabolites = metabolites, celltype = "Monocyte",
    genes = interferon, method = "block_glasso")
```

The helper above asks for `transform = "log_cpm"`, the base-2 logarithm of the
counts per million plus one. Either transform is computed from all genes of the
object; `genes` then names the genes that become nodes.

# A network for one cell type

`method = "block_glasso"` is the graphical lasso [@friedman2008] on the
correlation matrix of the features, with one penalty for pairs of features of
the same layer (`lambda_w`, default 0.3) and one for pairs of different layers
(`lambda_b`, default 0.5). `covariates` are regressed out of both layers
first.

```{r monocyte-network, eval=has("glasso")}
mono <- network("Monocyte", method = "block_glasso")
mono
```

The result is a `CelltypeNetworkResult`. Its parts are read with accessors:

```{r accessors, eval=has("glasso")}
networkCelltype(mono)
networkMethod(mono)
head(networkNodes(mono), 3)
dim(networkPrecision(mono))
sum(networkAdjacency(mono)) / 2
metadata(mono)[c("n_donors", "transform", "covariates")]
```

The penalties decide how many edges there are, within the layers and between
them:

```{r penalties, eval=has("glasso")}
looser <- network("Monocyte", method = "block_glasso", lambda_w = 0.2,
    lambda_b = 0.2)
rbind(default = unlist(metadata(mono)$edge_counts),
    looser = unlist(metadata(looser)$edge_counts))
```

```{r plot-network, eval=has("glasso", plot_packages)}
#| fig.cap: >-
#|   The network of monocytes at the looser penalties. Edges between a
#|   transcript and a metabolite are highlighted.
set.seed(1)
plot_celltype_network(looser, layout = "fr", label_top = 22L)
```

# Penalties chosen by stability

`method = "coglasso"` is the collaborative graphical lasso [@albanese2026],
which also has one penalty for pairs within a layer and one for pairs between
the layers, and a weight for the agreement of the layers. All three are chosen
from a grid by the stability of the edges under subsampling of the donors. The
grid and the number of subsamples are small here to keep the vignette short;
the defaults are a 15 by 15 grid and 20 subsamples.

```{r coglasso, eval=has_coglasso}
set.seed(1)
stable <- network("Monocyte", method = "coglasso", nlambda_w = 5L,
    nlambda_b = 5L, rep_num = 10L)
stable
unlist(metadata(stable)$selection)
```

coglasso takes the largest penalty of each grid from the data: the largest
correlation within a layer and the largest between the layers. When this
vignette was written, the within-layer penalty chosen was that largest value,
at which no two features of one layer are joined. The network then has edges
between the layers only because the choice ended at the edge of the grid, not
because the transcripts are unrelated to each other; the block graphical lasso
above joins many of them.

`networkStability()` returns, for every pair of features, the fraction of the
subsamples in which the pair was joined at the chosen penalties.

```{r stability, eval=has_coglasso}
scores <- networkStability(stable)
dim(scores)
table(cut(scores[upper.tri(scores)], c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
    include.lowest = TRUE))
```

```{r plot-stability, eval=has_coglasso && has("ggplot2")}
#| fig.cap: >-
#|   Pairs of features by the fraction of subsamples in which they were
#|   joined at the chosen penalties. Not every pair shown is an edge of the
#|   network.
plot_edge_stability(stable)
```

The two estimators need not agree, and with 43 donors the result of either
depends on its settings. When this vignette was written, a 4 by 4 grid and a
6 by 6 grid each gave a coglasso network other than the one above, and the
defaults of the function, a 15 by 15 grid and 20 subsamples, gave the same
one.

# Two cell types

`run_comparative_network()` sets networks of several cell types side by side.
It needs the same features in each. Naming the genes with `genes` provides
them, as long as each gene has counts in each cell type: a gene that is
constant across the donors of a cell type is left out of that network, with a
message. `top_var_genes`, the other way to limit the transcripts, takes the
most variable genes of each cell type, and these differ between cell types.

```{r comparison, eval=has("glasso")}
tcell <- network("T cell", method = "block_glasso")
comparison <- run_comparative_network(mono, tcell)
comparison
unlist(comparisonSummary(comparison)[c("n_total_edges", "n_shared",
    "n_differential")])
head(sharedEdges(comparison), 3)
head(diffEdges(comparison), 3)
vapply(celltypeSpecificEdges(comparison), nrow, integer(1))
```

`max_diff` is the difference between the partial correlations of an edge in
the two networks.

```{r plot-comparison, eval=has("glasso", "ggplot2")}
#| fig.cap: >-
#|   Edges that are in one of the two networks only, by the difference of
#|   their partial correlations.
plot_network_comparison(comparison)
```

The comparison is descriptive. It tests no edge and reports no p-value, and an
edge that is in one network and not in the other can be within the noise of
either estimate.

# Features associated with an exposure

`run_exposure_network()` works in two stages. It first selects, among the
genes of the cell type and the features of the second layer, those associated
with an exposure, and then estimates a network among the selected features
only. The exposure here is age. Sex is given as a covariate: the features are
screened by their rank correlation with age given sex, and sex is regressed
out of them before the network is estimated. The candidates are all genes of
the object and all
`r ncol(plasma)` plasma metabolites.

```{r exposure-network, eval=has("glasso")}
age_net <- run_exposure_network(x, log2(plasma), celltype = "Monocyte",
    exposure = "age", covariates = "sex_male",
    selection_method = "univariate", network_method = "block_glasso",
    transform = "log_cpm")
age_net
metadata(age_net)[c("n_total_features", "selection_method", "fdr_threshold")]
selected <- networkNodes(age_net)
table(selected$omic_layer)
selected$feature
```

`selection_method = "univariate"` keeps the features whose Spearman
correlation with the exposure, given the covariates, passes a false discovery
rate of 0.05 among the candidates that vary across the donors with a value of
the exposure; `"stability"` selects by stability
selection [@meinshausen2010] instead. The call stops when fewer than three
features are selected. `genes` names the candidate genes, as it names the nodes
of `run_celltype_network()`; fewer candidates leave fewer tests to adjust for.

The quantity that was tested is the partial rank correlation of a feature with
age given sex: the correlation of the two after the ranks of sex are regressed
out of the ranks of each. Regressing sex out of the values themselves and
ranking what is left would not do for a gene with few counts, whose many equal
values would then be ranked by sex. For the selected metabolites the
correlation is:

```{r exposure-sign, eval=has("glasso")}
chosen <- selected$feature[selected$omic_layer == "metabolite"]
donor_data <- as.data.frame(exposureData(x))
given_sex <- function(v) residuals(lm(rank(v) ~ rank(sex_male), donor_data))
ranks <- apply(plasma[, chosen, drop = FALSE], 2, given_sex)
round(cor(given_sex(donor_data$age), ranks)[1, ], 2)
```

Features that change with age in the same direction are correlated with each
other across donors of different ages, whatever else links them. The exposure
is not regressed out of the features and is not a node of the network, so an
edge between two features can reflect nothing more than the association that
both have with the exposure. The network does not estimate how the dependence
between features changes with the exposure.

# What a network does not show

Selecting features and estimating a network on the same donors overstates the
stability of the result; a network that is to be relied on needs donors that
took no part in the selection. Building a network within a cell type removes
the differences between broad cell types from the transcript values, but not
those between subtypes, and not the effects of sampling, capture and
annotation. And the graph is one of many that 43 donors are compatible with.
